title: Predicting when mild cognitive impairment may become dementia, as a window of years
paper_title: Multimodal Survival Transformer for Progression Window Estimation of Time to Dementia
date_note: HMSS 2026 (2nd Int. Conf. on Health Medical Systems and Services), IEEE Xplore, in press; the camera-ready PDF was built on 2 Oct 2026 but gives no conference date, so mid-October 2026 is a guess
venue: 2nd International Conference on Health Medical Systems and Services (HMSS 2026)
authors: David Calhas, Swarnendu Ghosh, Branko Šter, Vida Groznik, Dejan Georgiev, Aleksander Sadikov
summary: Instead of one guessed date, we predict a window of years for when mild cognitive impairment may progress to dementia, using brain scans and clinical records from 941 people.

body.p: When a person has Mild Cognitive Impairment, doctors would like to know when, if ever, it will turn into dementia. That time is hard to predict, so in this study we asked a model for a window of years instead of a single date. We tested three models on brain scans and clinical records from 941 participants of a large research study, the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI).

body.h2: Why one date does not work

body.p: Doctors stage the disease with the Clinical Dementia Rating, or CDR. Mild Cognitive Impairment corresponds to CDR 0.5, and dementia to CDR 1 or higher. The time we want to predict is how long a patient stays at 0.5.

Three things make that time hard to pin down. Patients are only seen at clinic visits, a median of 11.7 months apart, so the true moment of change falls somewhere between two visits. Experts often disagree on the rating. And some patients stop coming. A single predicted date pretends to a precision the data cannot give.

Each model reads a patient's T1 MRI brain scan, their clinical record and the history of visits. It outputs a survival curve: for every future year, the chance that the patient is still at CDR 0.5. Reading the curve at two points gives a window. For an 80% window, there is a 10% chance that progression comes before the window and a 10% chance that it comes after.

figure.alt: Flow diagram: inputs (MRI, clinical record, visit history) feed three survival models, which produce survival curves and prediction windows, which feed cluster analysis and a failure-prediction Expert.
figure.caption: The whole system: scans and records go into three models, whose outputs are used for ranking, windows, clusters and a network that tries to predict the model's own failures.

body.p: The first model, ResNet-18×4, is an ensemble of four image networks that read up to six scans per patient and combine them with the clinical record. The second, MST×4, is our multimodal survival transformer. It lets regions of the brain scan and items of the clinical record look at each other, using attention, and then links the visits of one patient over time. The third, MST-W, has an extra output that learns the window directly, trained to minimise the interval score: the window width plus a penalty for each year by which the true time falls outside it.

We trained on scans and records of 941 ADNI participants who were at CDR 0.5. Of them, 293 (31%) progressed to CDR 1 or higher. The median follow-up was 3 years. The scans of 1,018 other people were used only to pre-train the image part.

For ranking, the three models are equal. Ranking is measured by the concordance index: given two patients, how often the model gives the higher risk to the one who progresses first (0.5 is a coin toss). ResNet-18×4 and MST×4 both reached 0.813, and the MST-W curve 0.812. A model using the clinical data alone reached 0.792, a Cox model 0.773 and a random survival forest 0.783. Adding the scan to the clinical data raised the score by 0.021, but this was not significant after correcting for the many comparisons we made.

The windows are where the models differ. Both kinds reached their target coverage at 80% and 90%, and covered more than they promised at 50%. The directly trained windows were wider, 6.7 against 6.0 years at 80%. Over all patients they won the interval score, 7.51 against 7.89 for the curve (lower is better). For patients who actually progressed, the order flipped: 8.69 for the MST curve, 9.52 for the trained window.

figure.alt: Four small line charts comparing population, ResNet-18 curve, MST curve and MST-W trained windows at 50, 80 and 90 percent levels: coverage, median width, interval score for all patients, interval score for patients who progressed.
figure.caption: Coverage, width and interval score of the windows at three confidence levels. Grey is a window that ignores the patient, built from the whole population.

body.callout: For patients who progressed, windows read off the survival curve scored 8.69 against 9.52 for a trained window head (lower is better); the three models all ranked patients at 0.81.

body.p: The trained window gets its edge from patients who never progressed during follow-up: it pushes the upper bound beyond the last visit, which cannot be checked. The lower bound is the hard part. Among patients who progressed, 27% did so before the lower bound of the 80% window.

We also split the patients into groups. Groups built only from baseline information separated risk: 19%, 42% and 55% of their members progressed. Windows helped most in the groups where progression was common. Brain maps of the descriptive groups agree with the clinical picture. The clinically advanced group had the lowest scan signal in the hippocampi and the temporal poles, regions known to be affected in Alzheimer's disease.

figure.alt: Brain slices for three patient groups, coloured blue or red by tissue signal and by model attention, next to a pie chart of which clinical inputs matter most.
figure.caption: Where three patient groups differ in the scan, and where the model looks. Five current CDR domains carry 85% of the importance among clinical inputs.

body.p: Finally, we trained a second network, the Expert, to predict when the first model will fail. It added little. For window misses the model's own uncertainty points the wrong way, with an area under the curve of 0.40, and 0.60 once flipped. Confident patients are the ones whose windows miss.

The study uses ADNI only, a curated research cohort, and we have no test on an outside cohort. CDR 0.5 also includes very mild dementia. The clinical inputs include the CDR domains from which the target rating is built, so part of the signal is circular. The attention maps show where the network looks, not what causes its predictions. Windows are least reliable for patients with short follow-up. This is a research result, not a clinical tool.
Next, we plan to give each bound its own training objective, and to test the system on an external cohort, with ablations and a conformal baseline.
